_comment: Circuit knowledge, keyed by canonical slug (see track.py for the alias
resolution that maps rF2's names onto these).
name        how the booth says it
country     for the header and scene-setting
character   what the circuit DEMANDS — used as analyst colour
overtaking  where a pass actually happens, for battle commentary
facts       booth colour, third person, no first-person claims
corners     in lap order; track.corner(frac) indexes into this
NOTE ON VOICE: these are deliberately NOT written as an ex-driver's
personal memories. Chuck Brannigan raced NASCAR 1985-2006 — he did not
win at Spa in an F1 car, and lines claiming he did would contradict the
biography that makes him credible everywhere else. Where a first-person
note is appropriate, it is gated by discipline in the pools, not here.
`sectors` - three clauses, one per timing sector, saying what THAT part of
the lap asks of a driver. The engineer uses it when he can see which sector
you are losing time in.
Written per circuit rather than derived from the corner list, because sector
boundaries are not evenly spaced by corner count and naming a corner in the
wrong sector is exactly the small wrongness that stops him being believed.
A circuit without `sectors` gets no coaching at all, which is the correct
failure.
Each clause completes '...that is where it is going, <clause>' - so present
tense, no leading article, no terminal full stop.
A FACT MAY CARRY `year: [lo, hi]`, exactly as a dialogue line does, and is
then only offered for a LAYOUT inside that range. `Track.year` is scraped
from the rF2 folder name.
This matters more than it looks. A historic circuit is not a shorter
version of the modern one, it is a DIFFERENT ROAD. Spa in 1966 was over
fourteen kilometres of public road; the modern entry told the booth the lap
was 'over seven kilometres, the longest on the calendar' and it aired over
the 1966 circuit.
THE RULE: a fact about the PLACE - its history, its geography, what it was
built on, who died there - stays undated and is true of every layout. A
fact about the ROAD - how long it is, which corners it has, how fast it is
- carries a year range.
A layout with NO year in its folder name gets the undated facts only.
Fewer facts, none of them wrong.
`identity_only` - the booth can NAME this circuit and a calendar can point
at it, but there is no lore, so the scene-setting and fact lines never
fire. `fictional` marks the ones that are not real places at all: those
have no country, because inventing one would be inventing a fact about
somewhere that does not exist. A real circuit we simply know little about
still gets its country.
`corners_history` - corner lists for layouts that differ from the modern
one, each with a `year` range. `Track.corners()` picks the matching block.
The default `corners` list is the CURRENT road, and using it for a historic
layout names corners that do not exist: Silverstone's includes Village, the
Loop and the Wellington Straight, which are the Arena section built in
2010, and they were being named during a 1991 race.

spa.name: Spa-Francorchamps
spa.character: Fast, sweeping and utterly committed. Seven kilometres through the Ardennes forest, with more elevation change than anywhere else on the calendar.
spa.overtaking: Into Les Combes at the top of the hill, and into the Bus Stop chicane.
facts: Eau Rouge and Raidillon: a compression at the bottom, blind over the crest, and the car goes light exactly when you need it not to.

facts.t: The old circuit ran over fourteen kilometres on public roads through the Ardennes.

facts: The Kemmel straight after Raidillon is where the slipstream does its work.
Spa makes its own weather. It can be dry at La Source and raining at Stavelot.
Pouhon is a double-left taken far quicker than it looks, and it punishes a car that will not rotate.
The run from Eau Rouge to Les Combes climbs over forty metres.
Blanchimont is flat in a modern car and was a genuine corner in an older one.

facts.t: The lap is over seven kilometres, the longest on the Formula One calendar.
The circuit is long enough that it can be raining at one end and completely dry at the other.
This is the old Spa — over fourteen kilometres of public road through the Ardennes villages, and more than twice the length of the modern circuit.
The old circuit ran through Malmedy and Stavelot on ordinary roads, with houses, hedges and telegraph poles at the edge of it.
Average speeds here approached two hundred and forty kilometres an hour in the sixties, on a road with almost no barriers.
A Grand Prix here began in a rainstorm that caught half the field on the opening lap — Jackie Stewart was trapped in his car in a ditch, and it changed his view of safety for ever.

sectors: carrying speed up through Eau Rouge
rhythm through Pouhon and Stavelot
a tidy exit from the Bus Stop

monza.name: Monza
monza.character: The Temple of Speed. Long straights, heavy braking, minimum downforce — and a slipstream that makes every straight a negotiation.
monza.overtaking: Into the first chicane, and into Ascari if you are brave.
facts: Monza is the fastest permanent circuit in Formula One, with cars flat out for most of the lap.

facts.t: The old banking still stands in the trees, crumbling but visible from the modern track.
Low downforce here means the car is quick on the straights and nervous everywhere else.

facts: Lesmo one and two tighten as you go through, which is why so many cars run wide at the second.
The Parabolica is a long, patient right-hander where the exit onto the main straight is everything.

facts.t: Ascari is a fast left-right-left that rewards a car with a stable rear.
It has hosted a Grand Prix every year since 1950 bar one, more than any other circuit.
This is Monza before the chicanes — flat out almost the whole way, with slipstreaming packs of cars crossing the line together.
The banked oval was still standing and still used in this era, and the combined circuit ran on both.
Races here in the sixties were decided by the slipstream on the run to the line, and the winning margins were measured in hundredths.

sectors: the first chicane, easy to lock up
Ascari, the corner that makes the lap
patience on entry to Parabolica

zandvoort.name: Zandvoort
zandvoort.character: Narrow and relentless, built into the dunes, with barely a straight worth the name and almost nowhere to pass.
zandvoort.overtaking: Into Tarzan, and that is close to the whole list.
facts: Zandvoort is built in the dunes, and sand blows onto the circuit all weekend.
The track is narrow by modern standards, which is exactly why the racing is so close.
Track position matters more here than almost anywhere — the pit lane decides races Zandvoort will not.
Tarzan at the end of the main straight is the one real overtaking spot on the lap, and everything in a driver's afternoon is built around it.
Scheivlak is the corner the drivers talk about: fast, blind, downhill, and the sand is waiting if you get it wrong.
The circuit was laid out on roads the occupying army had built during the war, which is why it wanders the way it does.

facts.t: The final corner is banked at eighteen degrees, one of the steepest in Formula One, and cars can run side by side through it.
Hugenholtz is banked as well, and it loads the car up in a way that punishes anything understeering.
Two banked corners on one lap is almost unheard of — most circuits do not have a single one.
The banking was added so cars could follow each other through the last corner and still have a run to Tarzan. That was the entire point of it.
The last corner is flat and conventional here, so a driver who loses the exit has no way of staying with the car in front down the straight.
Hugenholtz is a tight, awkward left with no banking to help the car turn — get it wrong and the whole middle sector is compromised.
This is a circuit that rewards a driver who can carry speed without the road helping him do it.

sectors: a late apex at Tarzan
the blind stuff through the dunes
power on early in the banked last corner
a late apex at Tarzan
the blind stuff through the dunes
a clean exit from the last corner, because there is no banking to save it

hockenheim.name: Hockenheim
hockenheim.character: A stop-start rhythm — heavy braking zones linked by short bursts, then a stadium section that never lets up.
hockenheim.overtaking: Into the hairpin, and into the Spitzkehre at the end of the long run.
facts: The Motodrom stadium section packs the crowd right against the fence — the noise inside it is extraordinary.

facts.t: Traction out of the hairpin is what sets the lap up, because the run afterwards is long.

facts: The Sachskurve is a long right that loads the left front hard and hurts a car with any understeer.

facts.t: Braking stability into the Spitzkehre is worth more here than outright downforce.
The original circuit ran deep into the forest on enormous straights; the modern lap is a fraction of its length.

facts: Jim Clark was killed here in a Formula Two race in 1968, on the old forest layout.

facts.t: This is the old Hockenheim — two enormous straights running deep into the forest, joined by chicanes, and then the stadium.
The forest section was so fast that the cars spent most of the lap at full throttle and the stadium was the only real cornering.

sectors: traction out of the slow corners
braking stability into the stadium
the stadium section, tight and banked

interlagos.name: Interlagos
interlagos.character: Short, bumpy and run anti-clockwise, with a long uphill drag to the line that makes the last corner the most important on the lap.
interlagos.overtaking: Into turn one at the bottom of the hill, and into the Senna S.
facts: Interlagos runs anti-clockwise, which loads the drivers' necks the opposite way to almost everywhere else.
The circuit is built on uneven ground and has never been smooth — the bumps are part of its character.
The climb from Juncao to the line is where a good exit turns into an overtake at turn one.
It is one of the shortest laps in racing, so traffic arrives constantly.
Sao Paulo weather changes fast, and a dry race here has often ended wet.
The circuit runs anticlockwise, which is unusual and physically demanding over a race distance.
It sits on a plateau around eight hundred metres up, so the cars run slightly more wing than the layout suggests.
The lap is short, so traffic in qualifying is a genuine problem and the field is compressed.
The surface is famously bumpy, and the run up the hill to the line is far steeper than television makes it look.
sectors: turning in late at the Senna S
the infield climb, slow and technical
a patient exit from the last corner

lemans.name: Le Mans
lemans.character: Thirteen kilometres of public road and circuit, most of it flat out. Gearing, aerodynamics and bravery, and very little else.
lemans.overtaking: Into the Mulsanne corner, and under braking for the chicanes.
facts: The Mulsanne straight ran uninterrupted for nearly six kilometres before the chicanes were added in 1990.
Most of the lap is public road, closed for the race and open to traffic the rest of the year.
The Porsche Curves are among the fastest sequences in motorsport and the least forgiving.
Cars spend the vast majority of the lap at full throttle, which makes gearing and drag the whole setup.
Indianapolis and Arnage arrive after enormous speed and demand the car be genuinely slowed.
Night running here is a different circuit entirely — the braking markers simply are not there.
The race runs through the night, and drivers deal with traffic across several classes at wildly different speeds.
sectors: braking into the Dunlop chicane
patience down the Mulsanne
the Porsche curves, pure commitment

daytona.name: Daytona
daytona.character: Thirty-one degrees of banking and a pack that runs nose to tail. Aerodynamics decide it, and the draft decides the aerodynamics.
daytona.overtaking: Anywhere, with help. Nowhere, without it.
facts: The banking at Daytona is thirty-one degrees — steep enough that walking up it is difficult.
In the draft, the car behind is quicker than the car in front, which is why the lead changes so often.
The road course cuts through the infield and rejoins the banking, and the two halves need opposite things from the car.
The tri-oval start-finish means cars are still turning as they cross the line.
Pack racing here is a cooperative sport until the last lap, and then it very much is not.
The twenty-four hour race here is run partly on the banking and partly through an infield road course.
Sports cars run at nearly full throttle around the banking, and the racing there is entirely about the draft.
The lake in the infield was dug out to build the banking.
sectors: momentum and traffic on the banking
the infield, the only real driving here
the exit back onto the banking

monaco.name: Monaco
monaco.character: Barriers everywhere, no run-off, and a lap where the difference between quick and crashed is a few centimetres.
monaco.overtaking: Into the Nouvelle Chicane, and realistically nowhere else.

facts.t: Monaco has no run-off. A mistake is a barrier, every single time.

facts: The tunnel takes the car from bright light to dark and back at maximum speed.
Qualifying matters more here than at any other circuit, because passing is close to impossible.

facts.t: The barriers at the swimming pool section move closer as the weekend goes on, or at least they seem to.

facts: The climb to Casino Square is blind at the crest and the car goes light exactly at turn-in.

facts.t: Rascasse and Anthony Noghes are slow enough to look easy and tight enough to catch anybody.

facts: The circuit has been used since 1929 and the layout has barely changed in principle.

facts.t: It is the slowest circuit on the calendar and the only one where the cars run maximum downforce all weekend.
This is Monaco before the swimming pool complex — the circuit ran straight along the harbour front to the Gasworks hairpin.
There were no barriers worth the name in this era, and the harbour was one wrong move away for the whole run along the quay.
The old circuit finished with the Gasworks hairpin, a slow right-hander that no longer exists.

sectors: Sainte Devote, it sets up the whole hill
the harbour chicane after the tunnel
the swimming pool, millimetres either side

bathurst.name: Mount Panorama
bathurst.character: A mountain with a road on it. Enormous elevation, concrete walls the whole way, and a top section barely wide enough for one car.
bathurst.overtaking: Into Hell Corner, and at the bottom of Conrod under braking for the Chase.
facts: Mount Panorama climbs and drops one hundred and seventy-four metres in a single lap.
Skyline drops away so steeply that the car is unloaded right where you commit to it.
The Esses across the top are lined with concrete and offer nothing at all if you get it wrong.
Conrod Straight is long enough that gearing for it costs you everywhere on the mountain.
The Cutting is steep, blind and uphill, and it eats cars that arrive badly positioned.
The circuit is a public road for most of the year, and there are houses and campsites alongside it.
The climb up the mountain and the descent through the Esses have almost no run-off at all.
Conrod Straight runs for nearly two kilometres before the Chase, which is the heaviest braking point on the lap.
sectors: across the top, no margin at all
the descent, it does not forgive
the Chase, hardest stop on the mountain

kyalami.name: Kyalami
kyalami.character: High altitude, big elevation and long fast corners. The thin air costs power and hurts cooling, and the lap flows in a way few modern circuits do.
kyalami.overtaking: Into Crowthorne at the end of the main straight, and into the Esses.
facts: Kyalami sits over fifteen hundred metres above sea level, and the thin air costs a naturally aspirated engine real power.
Cooling is a genuine problem here because there is simply less air to work with.
The circuit was redesigned in the nineties, and again more recently, but the character of the run down to Crowthorne survived.
The climb from Barbecue up through the Esses is one of the better sequences anywhere.
The main straight drops away downhill, so cars arrive at Crowthorne carrying more speed than the numbers suggest.
Altitude affects aerodynamics as well as power — there is less downforce for the same wing angle.
The original layout had an enormously long main straight; the modern circuit is shorter and more technical.
The 1982 race was preceded by a drivers' strike over superlicence terms, and they barricaded themselves in a hotel.
The climb through the middle sector is steep enough to flatter a car with good traction.
sectors: commitment through the fast opening corners
uphill braking through the middle
the exit of the final complex

silverstone.name: Silverstone
silverstone.character: Fast, open and flowing. A high-speed circuit on an old airfield where aerodynamic balance decides everything.
silverstone.overtaking: Into Stowe, and into Brooklands at the end of the Wellington straight.
facts: Silverstone was built on a wartime airfield, and the layout still follows the old runways.

facts.t: Copse is one of the fastest corners in racing and is taken very close to flat.

facts: The Maggotts-Becketts-Chapel sequence changes direction repeatedly at enormous speed and is a genuine test of a chassis.
It is exposed, and the wind changes the balance from session to session.
Stowe rewards a car that can be braked late and still turn.
The first World Championship Grand Prix was held here in 1950.

facts.t: This is the first big redesign of the circuit — the old flat-out blast was broken up by the Becketts complex and the Priory and Luffield sequence.
Before this redesign Silverstone was one of the fastest circuits in the world, and the changes were made precisely to slow it down.
Nigel Mansell once gave Ayrton Senna a lift back to the pits on his sidepod after Senna ran out of fuel.

sectors: Copse and Maggotts, all commitment
Stowe, braking into a corner that keeps turning
the exit of Club onto the straight

suzuka.name: Suzuka
suzuka.character: A figure of eight, and the most complete test of a car anywhere — high-speed direction change, slow hairpins and a corner that never stops turning.
suzuka.overtaking: Into the chicane at the end of the lap, and into turn one.
facts: Suzuka is the only figure-of-eight circuit in top-level motorsport — the back straight crosses over the first section.
The Esses in the first sector are a rhythm section; get the first one wrong and the whole sequence is compromised.
130R is a long, fast left taken flat in a modern car and very much not in an older one.
Spoon Curve is a double apex where patience on entry pays on the long run to 130R.
The circuit was designed as a Honda test track, which is why it demands so much of a chassis.
It was built by Honda in 1962 as a test track, and the layout was designed by a Dutchman, John Hugenholtz.
130R is a left-hander taken close to flat, and it is one of the fastest corners in the sport.
sectors: the esses, get the first one right
Degner and the hairpin back to back
commitment through 130R

imola.name: Imola
imola.character: Old-school, anti-clockwise and kerb-dependent. Narrow, with walls close and very little margin.
imola.overtaking: Into the Tamburello chicane, and into Rivazza.
facts: Imola runs anti-clockwise, one of only a handful of circuits that do.
Tamburello was a flat-out left-hander before the chicane was added.
Acque Minerali drops downhill into the braking zone, which unsettles the car right where you need it stable.
Rivazza is a double-left downhill, and the second part decides the run to the line.
The circuit runs anticlockwise, which is rare and adds to how physical it is over a distance.
It is named after Enzo Ferrari and his son Dino, and it sits a few miles from the Ferrari factory.
The kerbs here are aggressive, and using them properly through the chicanes is most of the lap time.
sectors: kerbs through the first two chicanes
downhill braking at Acque Minerali
Rivazza and the last chicanes

nurburgring.name: the Nurburgring
nurburgring.character: The modern GP circuit — technical, stop-start, and always in the shadow of the old track next door.
nurburgring.overtaking: Into the Michael Schumacher S, and into the Dunlop hairpin.
facts: The modern Nurburgring shares a paddock with the Nordschleife, which runs to over twenty kilometres.
The Eifel mountains bring their own weather and it can change within a single lap.
The first-corner complex is heavy braking into a tight right, and traction out of it sets up the lap.
This is the modern Grand Prix circuit, built in 1984 alongside the old Nordschleife rather than as part of it.
The Eifel weather is the real character of the place — it can be dry on one side of the circuit and wet on the other.
The first corner is a tight right-hander at the end of a short run, and it has decided a lot of races.
The circuit has hosted Grands Prix under three different names, including the European and the Luxembourg.
sectors: traction out of the slow first sector
confidence in the front end mid-lap
the slow stuff, once the tyres have gone

nordschleife.name: the Nordschleife
nordschleife.character: Twenty kilometres, more than seventy corners and a hundred metres of elevation. There is no other circuit like it and there never will be.
nordschleife.overtaking: Wherever you dare, and traffic makes that decision for you.
facts: The Nordschleife runs to over twenty kilometres with more than seventy named corners.
Jackie Stewart called it the Green Hell, and the name stuck.
The elevation change across a lap is roughly three hundred metres.
The Karussell is a banked concrete ditch, and cars drop into it rather than drive around it.
Flugplatz gets its name for a reason — the car genuinely leaves the ground.
A lap takes long enough that weather at one end can differ from the other.
Formula One left after 1976, when Niki Lauda's accident made the circuit's lack of marshalling impossible to justify.
sectors: rhythm through Hatzenbach
the blind crests, they never stop
the long run home, stay awake

indianapolis.name: Indianapolis
indianapolis.character: Four identical corners and two and a half miles of history. On the oval it is about trimming out; on the road course it is a different circuit entirely.
indianapolis.overtaking: Into turn one on the oval, and into turn one of the infield on the road course.
facts: The Speedway opened in 1909 and was originally surfaced with over three million bricks.
A yard of the original brick surface remains at the start-finish line.
All four turns are identical in radius and banking, which sounds simple and is not.
On the oval, a car trimmed for speed is a car that will not hold on in traffic.
The Formula One circuit used the banking in the opposite direction to the Indianapolis 500, running clockwise through the infield.
The banking is far steeper than it looks on television, and the cars are at full throttle all the way round it.
sectors: braking into the infield off the banking
the infield, slow and technical
momentum back onto the banking

roadamerica.name: Road America
roadamerica.character: Four miles of long straights and fast, open corners through Wisconsin farmland. Big braking zones and real elevation.
roadamerica.overtaking: Into turn five, into turn eight, and into the Carousel.
facts: Road America is over four miles long and has barely changed since 1955.
The straights are long enough that gearing and drag dominate the setup.
The Carousel is a long, patient right where the exit matters far more than the entry.
Canada Corner is a heavy braking zone and one of the best passing places in North America.
The elevation change through the Kink and up to Canada Corner is significant and not obvious on a map.
The lap is over four miles, one of the longest permanent road courses in North America.
The Kink is a fast left that is taken flat in most machinery and is genuinely intimidating in all of it.
The circuit has barely changed since it opened in 1955, which is why it still feels like an old road course.
sectors: brake stability into the heavy stops
the Carousel, do not get greedy
the Kink, then one last big stop

montreal.name: Montreal
montreal.character: A stop-start park circuit with walls close and traction at a premium. Brakes take a beating and the kerbs are unforgiving.
montreal.overtaking: Into the final chicane, and into the turn ten hairpin.
facts: Circuit Gilles Villeneuve is built on an island in the Saint Lawrence river.
The hairpin is the slowest corner and leads onto the longest straight, so its exit is worth a great deal.
The wall on the exit of the final chicane is known as the Wall of Champions — it caught Damon Hill, Michael Schumacher and Jacques Villeneuve in the same afternoon in 1999.
The circuit is named after Gilles Villeneuve, who won here in 1978 in his first season with Ferrari.
Brakes take more punishment here than almost anywhere: it is a series of heavy stops with very little time to cool in between.
The island the circuit sits on was built for Expo 67, and the rowing basin from the 1976 Olympics runs alongside it.

facts.t: This is the circuit before the pit complex was rebuilt, with the old narrow pit lane still in place.

sectors: turning in early and getting the power down
the hairpin exit onto the back straight
the last chicane, kerb without the wall

bahrain.name: Bahrain
bahrain.character: Heavy braking, abrasive surface and desert heat. Rear tyre management is the whole race.
bahrain.overtaking: Into turn one, into turn four, and into turn eleven.
facts: The surface at Bahrain is abrasive and the rear tyres pay for it all race.
It gets run into the evening, and the track temperature falls sharply once the sun goes down.
Sand blows onto the circuit and the grip off-line is genuinely poor.
There are three big braking zones with realistic passing chances, which is more than most modern circuits offer.
The heavy braking into turn one is the best overtaking opportunity of the lap and the biggest stop on the circuit.
Rear tyre wear is the defining problem here — the traction zones are relentless and the surface is abrasive.
sectors: the big stop into turn one
the middle corners, it is all rear tyre
the quick last sector, if the tyres are alive

sepang.name: Sepang
sepang.character: Wide, hot and humid, with two enormous straights and a pair of very long corners that punish a tired front tyre.
sepang.overtaking: Into turn one, and into turn fifteen at the end of the back straight.
facts: Sepang is brutally hot and humid, and it is as hard on the driver as on the car.
The two long straights are joined by hairpins, which makes drag the central setup compromise.
Turn five and turn nine are long, patient corners that hurt the front left.
Heat and humidity here are close to Singapore's, and afternoon thunderstorms are almost a fixture.
The first two corners are far longer than they look, and both reward patience over commitment.
The circuit was Hermann Tilke's first Formula One design and set the template for many that followed.
sectors: the two long opening corners
the middle sector, hottest the tyres get
braking stability at the two hairpins

portimao.name: Portimao
portimao.character: A rollercoaster. Blind crests, steep drops and almost no flat ground anywhere on the lap.
portimao.overtaking: Into turn one, and into turn five.
facts: Portimao has more elevation change than almost any modern circuit — the lap is genuinely a rollercoaster.
Several corners are blind over a crest, and you commit before you can see the apex.
The final corner drops downhill onto the main straight, so its exit is worth a lot.
The circuit rises and falls so dramatically that several corners are taken completely blind over a crest.
The surface was newly laid when Formula One first visited and offered almost no grip at all until it rubbered in.
It is one of very few modern circuits with genuine elevation change designed in rather than engineered out.
sectors: the blind crest into turn one
the rollercoaster, it never settles
patience in that long last corner

estoril.name: Estoril
estoril.character: A long final corner onto a long straight — get that wrong and you lose the lap twice over.
estoril.overtaking: Into turn one at the end of the main straight.
facts: The final corner at Estoril is long and leads onto the main straight, which makes it the most important on the lap.
The circuit is exposed and coastal, and the wind swings the balance around.
Estoril hosted the Portuguese Grand Prix through the eighties and nineties.
The 1984 championship was settled here by half a point, the closest margin in the sport's history.
Ayrton Senna took his first Grand Prix win at Estoril in 1985, in appalling wet conditions, by over a minute.
sectors: being tidy rather than brave early on
rhythm through the middle
the long last corner onto the straight

limerock.name: Lime Rock Park
limerock.character: Barely a mile and a half, seven corners, and no real straight. Rhythm and momentum, with lap times counted in fractions.
limerock.overtaking: Into the Left-Hander, and under braking at Big Bend.
facts: Lime Rock is one of the shortest road courses in professional racing at well under two miles.
There is almost no straight, so momentum matters more than power.
The Uphill and the Downhill are exactly what they sound like, and both are taken faster than they look.
Traffic arrives constantly because the lap is so short.
The lap is barely a mile and a half, one of the shortest in professional racing, so traffic is constant.
There are only seven corners, and a mistake at any of them costs a noticeable fraction of the lap.
Local noise ordinances mean racing here on a Sunday has historically been restricted.
sectors: commitment over the uphill crest
braking on the downhill
the run to the line, it is a short lap

portland.name: Portland
portland.character: A long back straight into a tight chicane, and a first-corner complex that has produced more chaos than almost any other.
portland.overtaking: Into the Festival Curves at the end of the front straight.
facts: The Festival Curves chicane at the end of the main straight has produced some spectacular first-lap incidents.
The back straight is long enough to make the slipstream a real factor.
The surface is bumpy in places and the circuit is flat, which makes braking references hard to find.
The circuit is flat, fast and unusually smooth, and it sits on the site of Vanport, a town destroyed by flooding in 1948.
It is one of the few road courses where a slipstream down the main straight genuinely decides positions.
sectors: kerbs through the Festival chicane
rhythm through the fast middle
the long exit from the last corner

longford.name: Longford
longford.character: Public roads, a railway crossing and a bridge. One of the fastest and most dangerous circuits ever raced on.
longford.overtaking: On the long straights, if you have the courage for it.
facts: Longford ran on public roads in Tasmania and included a level crossing and a wooden bridge.
It was among the fastest circuits in the world in its day, with very high average speeds.
Cars crossed a railway line at genuine speed, which tells you most of what you need to know about the era.
The circuit closed in 1968 — the roads are still there and still open to traffic.

facts.t: This is very close to the last configuration ever raced here.

sectors: momentum down the straights
the bridges and the crossing
the run home, flat and committed

shanghai.name: Shanghai
shanghai.character: A circuit of two extremes — an opening corner that spirals inward for an age, and then one of the longest straights in the sport into a heavy stop.
facts: The first corner is a long right-hander that keeps tightening, and a driver is turning for what feels like an eternity before it opens again.
The back straight is around one and a quarter kilometres and ends in one of the heaviest braking zones of the year.
The layout is said to be drawn from the Chinese character shang, meaning above.
The circuit was built on marshland, and the ground shifting underneath it has caused surface problems ever since.
The combination of the long opening corner and the long straight makes setting the car up here a genuine compromise.
shanghai.overtaking: Into turn fourteen at the end of the back straight, and into turn six.
sectors: the long spiral into turn one and out of turn three
the middle complex and the hairpin
the enormous straight and the stop at the end of it

jeddah.name: Jeddah
jeddah.character: The fastest street circuit in the sport — twenty-seven corners, most of them barely a lift, with walls close enough to touch and almost nothing you can see through.
facts: This is the fastest street circuit in Formula One, with average speeds over two hundred and fifty kilometres an hour.
There are twenty-seven corners, and a great many of them are taken flat or close to it.
The walls sit right against the racing line, and several of the fast corners are genuinely blind.
It is one of the longest laps on the current calendar.
Because the corners are quick and the walls are close, a small mistake here is rarely a small mistake.
jeddah.overtaking: Into turn one, and into turn twenty-seven.
sectors: the opening corners and the walls that follow them
the blind fast stuff through the middle
the last sequence, and the run to the line

miami.name: Miami
miami.character: A circuit laid out around a stadium car park — fast sweeps at either end and a slow, awkward technical section under the flyovers in the middle.
facts: The circuit is built around the Hard Rock Stadium, and the paddock sits inside it.
The first running of the race featured a marina with painted water and plastic boats, which did not survive the mockery.
The middle sector runs under road flyovers and is markedly slower and more awkward than the rest of the lap.
The surface was originally very smooth and short on grip, and has needed reworking.
The two long straights make this a low-downforce circuit despite the slow middle section.
miami.overtaking: Into turn eleven, into turn seventeen, and into turn one.
sectors: the fast opening sweeps
the awkward stuff under the flyovers
the long straights and the stops at the end of them

hungaroring.name: the Hungaroring
hungaroring.character: Tight, twisty and relentless — a circuit often called Monaco without the walls, where track position is worth more than pace.
facts: Overtaking here is famously difficult, so qualifying matters more than at almost any other permanent circuit.
The Hungaroring held the first Formula One race staged behind the Iron Curtain, in 1986.
It is used rarely, so the racing line is dusty and slippery early in a weekend and improves lap by lap.
The race falls in August, and the combination of heat and constant corners is punishing on tyres and drivers alike.
There is barely a straight worth the name — the lap is one corner into the next for the whole distance.
hungaroring.overtaking: Into turn one, and it is very hard anywhere else.
sectors: the downhill stop into turn one
the twisting middle, where rhythm is everything
the last corners, and getting the drive onto the straight

baku.name: Baku
baku.character: A street circuit of two halves — a medieval castle section barely wide enough for one car, and then the longest flat-out run in the sport.
facts: The run from the final corner to turn one is over two kilometres, and it is the longest full-throttle stretch in Formula One.
The castle section climbs through the walls of Baku's old city and is the narrowest piece of road on the calendar — around seven and a half metres.
Teams run their lowest downforce of the year here, which makes the cars quick on the straight and difficult everywhere else.
The old city walls are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the circuit runs right through them.
Low downforce plus close walls has made this one of the most eventful races of the modern era.
baku.overtaking: Into turn one at the end of the long straight, and into turn three.
sectors: the heavy stop into turn one and the run up to the castle
the castle section, and there is no room for error at all
the long blast to the line, where slipstream is everything

singapore.name: Marina Bay
singapore.character: A night race on public streets — hot, humid, bumpy and nearly two hours long. The most physically demanding race of the year, and the walls never move.
facts: Singapore staged the first night race in Formula One history, in 2008.
It is regularly the longest race of the season by time, and has more than once run up against the two-hour limit.
The heat and humidity make this the most physically demanding event of the year — drivers lose several kilos over a race distance.
The circuit runs on public roads, and the surface is bumpy in a way permanent circuits never are.
Safety cars here are close to a certainty, because the walls are everywhere and there is no run-off to speak of.
singapore.overtaking: Into turn seven, into turn fourteen, and into turn one.
sectors: the opening corners and the first walls
the twisting middle, where the bumps are worst
the last sequence, and concentration when you are exhausted

cota.name: the Circuit of the Americas
cota.character: A circuit built from other circuits — a blind uphill first corner, a copy of the Silverstone esses, and a long back straight into a heavy stop.
facts: Turn one is a blind uphill left-hander with something like forty metres of climb from the grid, and drivers cannot see the apex on the way in.
The esses through the first sector were modelled on the Maggotts and Becketts sequence at Silverstone.
The circuit deliberately borrows corners from several others, including Hockenheim and Istanbul.
The ground beneath it has moved since it was built, and the surface has needed repeated attention because of the bumps.
The long back straight into the turn eleven hairpin is one of the best overtaking places in the sport.
cota.overtaking: Into turn twelve at the end of the back straight, and into turn one.
sectors: the blind climb into turn one, then rhythm through the esses
the hairpin and the long straight after it
the slow final complex, and a tidy exit

mexico.name: Mexico City
mexico.character: The highest circuit in the sport by a distance. Thin air means less downforce, less cooling and enormous straight-line speed — the cars run maximum wing and still go faster than anywhere else.
facts: Mexico City sits around two thousand two hundred metres above sea level, making this comfortably the highest circuit on the calendar.
The thin air costs the cars roughly a quarter of their downforce, so teams run their biggest wings here and still record some of the highest top speeds of the year.
Cooling is the real problem at this altitude — there is simply less air to take heat out of the engine and the brakes.
The stadium section runs through the old Foro Sol baseball stadium, with grandstands on both sides.
The run from the grid to turn one is one of the longest in Formula One.
mexico.overtaking: Into turn one at the end of the long run, and into turn four.
sectors: the enormous run to turn one and the first complex
the esses, where the thin air costs you downforce
the stadium section, slow and tight and very loud

vegas.name: Las Vegas
vegas.character: A night race down the Strip — enormous straights, minimal downforce, and the coldest track temperatures in the sport, which makes simply getting a tyre to work the whole problem.
facts: The circuit runs at night down the Las Vegas Strip, past the casinos.
It is one of the fastest circuits on the calendar, with very long straights and low-downforce set-ups.
The cold is the real story here — track temperatures at night in the desert are the lowest all season, and getting the tyres into their window is genuinely difficult.
Because the tyres struggle to switch on, a single lap in qualifying can be worth an enormous amount of time.
Las Vegas hosted Formula One in the early eighties as well, on a completely different circuit in a car park.
vegas.overtaking: Into turn fourteen at the end of the Strip, and into turn five.
sectors: the opening corners, with tyres that are not ready
the long straights and the fast sweeps
the last corners, and the cold is still against you

losail.name: Losail
losail.character: A fast, flowing desert circuit built for motorcycles, run under floodlights, and famously hard on tyres.
facts: Losail was built in 2004 for motorcycle racing, and the flowing layout still reflects that.
It is a floodlit circuit — the whole race is run under lights.
The long, fast corners load the tyres so consistently that Formula One has twice had to impose stint limits here.
Sand blowing across the circuit is a constant problem, and grip changes with the wind.
There is very little slow-corner respite: the lap is one medium-to-high speed corner after another.
losail.overtaking: Into turn one, and it is difficult almost everywhere else.
sectors: the stop into turn one and the sweeps after it
the fast middle, and it never lets the tyres cool
the last corners onto the main straight

sochi.name: Sochi
sochi.character: A long, smooth lap around an Olympic park — one enormous left-hander early on, and very little tyre wear anywhere.
facts: The circuit was laid out around the Olympic Park built for the 2014 Winter Games.
Turn three is an extremely long left-hander that wraps around the Medals Plaza, and it goes on far longer than it first appears.
The surface is unusually smooth, and tyre wear here is among the lowest of any circuit.
Long straights joined by ninety-degree corners make this a circuit where traction and braking matter more than flow.
It is no longer on the Formula One calendar.
sochi.overtaking: Into turn two, and into turn thirteen.
sectors: the stop into turn two and the enormous turn three
the long straights and the square corners joining them
the twisting final sector

istanbul.name: Istanbul Park
istanbul.character: An anticlockwise lap with one of the great corners in modern racing — a long left-hander with four apexes that loads the car for an age.
facts: Istanbul Park runs anticlockwise, which is unusual and puts the loading on the opposite side of a driver's neck.
Turn eight is a single left-hander with four apexes, and cars are in it long enough for the loading to become an endurance question.
The circuit was designed by Hermann Tilke and opened in 2005.
It dropped off the calendar and returned briefly, which means very few current drivers have much running here.
istanbul.overtaking: Into turn twelve, and into turn one.
sectors: the downhill entry to turn one
turn eight, and it goes on far longer than it looks
the run home, and traction out of the last corner

albertpark.name: Albert Park
albertpark.character: A park circuit on public roads, quick and flowing, with a surface that is green on Friday and rubbered-in by Sunday.
facts: Albert Park is a public road circuit — the lake road is open traffic for most of the year.
It has opened the Formula One season more often than any other circuit outside Europe.
The lap runs anticlockwise around Albert Park Lake, and the water is on the inside for most of it.
Because the roads are barely used for racing, grip climbs dramatically across a weekend.
The surface changes character as the weekend goes on: green and slippery early, rubbered in and quick by the end.
Everything here is temporary — the barriers, the grandstands, the pit buildings — and it is all taken away again afterwards.

facts.t: The chicane at turn nine breaks up what would otherwise be the quickest part of the lap, and getting the kerbs right there is worth real time.
This is a stop-start lap: quick corners, then a chicane, then quick corners again, and the car has to be settled for both.
The circuit is narrow through the middle sector, so a driver who is quick there is still stuck behind anyone he cannot pass into turn one.
Turn one is tight and the run down to it is long, which is why almost every move here happens in the same place.
Several corners were widened and the old turn nine chicane taken out, which made the lap markedly faster.
Taking the chicane out turned the middle of the lap into a flat-out run, and the lap record fell by several seconds because of it.

albertpark.overtaking: Into turn one, into turn three, and into turn eleven.
sectors: a clean run through the first three corners
the fast middle sweeps, and trusting the front end
the last corners, and a good exit onto the straight
a tidy entry to turn one, because the whole lap starts there
the chicane, and getting on the kerbs without unsettling the car
the last corners, and a good exit onto the straight

catalunya.name: Barcelona-Catalunya
catalunya.character: The circuit every team knows best, because they tested here for decades. Long corners, a hard time for the front-left, and wind that moves the balance from session to session.
facts: Formula One teams used Barcelona for winter testing for decades, which means the data on this circuit runs deeper than anywhere else.
Turn three is a long, long right-hander that loads the front-left tyre harder than almost any corner in the sport.
The chicane added in 2007 was removed again for 2023, restoring the original fast final corner.
The wind direction here changes the car's balance noticeably, and it rarely blows the same way twice in a weekend.
Because everybody knows it so well, a driver who is quick here is genuinely quick rather than lucky.
catalunya.overtaking: Into turn one, and into turn ten.
sectors: the heavy stop into turn one and the long turn three
the technical middle, where the front tyre gives up
the last corners onto the main straight

redbullring.name: Red Bull Ring
redbullring.character: A very short lap with very few corners and a great deal of elevation — barely a minute of running, climbing and dropping the whole way.
facts: The lap is one of the shortest on the calendar, and a Formula One car gets round it in a little over a minute.
There are only around ten corners, which means the field is compressed and traffic in qualifying is a genuine problem.
The climb out of turn one is steep enough that the run to turn three is effectively uphill all the way.
The circuit was previously the Osterreichring and then the A1-Ring, and the current layout is much shorter than the original.
With a lap this brief, three DRS zones and heavy braking, the gaps here are tiny and the racing is usually close.
redbullring.overtaking: Into turn three, into turn four, and into turn one.
sectors: the climb out of turn one
the fast middle and the crest at turn six
the downhill run home, and it is over very quickly

paulricard.name: Paul Ricard
paulricard.character: A test track turned Grand Prix circuit, ringed by painted run-off designed to slow a car down rather than let it slide. The Mistral straight is the feature, and Signes at the end of it is barely a lift.
facts: The blue and red stripes are not decoration — the painted surface is deliberately abrasive, and it is there to slow a car that has run wide.
The Mistral straight is over a kilometre long and is usually split by a chicane.
Signes, at the end of the Mistral, is a right-hander taken at enormous speed.
Paul Ricard spent years as a test circuit, and it has an unusual number of possible layout configurations.
The run-off is so generous that a mistake here costs time rather than a car, which changes how drivers attack it.
paulricard.overtaking: Into the Mistral chicane, and into turn one.
sectors: the opening corners and the run to the Mistral
Signes and the braking into Beausset
the twisty final section back to the line

yasmarina.name: Yas Marina
yasmarina.character: A race that starts in daylight and finishes under floodlights, on a circuit reprofiled to make it flow — long straights, heavy stops and a banked corner around the marina.
facts: The race starts at sunset and finishes under floodlights, so the track temperature falls throughout — the car at the end is not the car at the start.
The pit lane exit runs underneath the circuit through a tunnel, which is unique in Formula One.
The layout was heavily reprofiled for 2021: the old slow chicanes went, the hairpins were opened up and turn nine was banked.
The Yas Hotel is built over the circuit, and the cars pass underneath it.
It has closed the season more often than any other circuit in the modern era.
yasmarina.overtaking: Into turn five, into turn nine, and into turn six.
sectors: the opening chicane and the first straight
the two long straights and the heavy stops
the banked marina section, in the dark

botniaring.name: Botniaring
botniaring.character: A short, flat Finnish club circuit — quick, simple and utterly unforgiving of a scruffy exit, because the straights are long enough to punish one.
facts: Botniaring sits near Kurikka in western Finland and is one of the country's main permanent circuits.
The lap is short and flat, so the field compresses quickly and traffic is a constant problem.
It is used heavily for national touring car and motorcycle racing rather than international events.
botniaring.overtaking: Into the hairpin, and into turn one.
sectors: a clean exit onto the first straight
the technical middle
the last corner, and the drive to the line

maastricht.name: Maastricht
maastricht.character: A temporary street circuit through a Dutch city — narrow, walled and bumpy, with almost no room to correct a mistake.
facts: Maastricht is a street layout rather than a permanent circuit, laid out on public roads through the city.
The surface is ordinary road, so the bumps and the camber are what a car has to be set up around.
Walls sit close to the racing line for most of the lap, which makes qualifying position worth a great deal.
maastricht.overtaking: Into the heavy braking zones, and almost nowhere else.
sectors: the opening chicane and the walls after it
the narrow middle section
the run home over the bumps

atlanta.name: Atlanta Motorsports Park
atlanta.character: A modern American club circuit with real elevation change, designed by Hermann Tilke as a private members' course.
facts: Atlanta Motorsports Park was designed by Hermann Tilke and opened in 2012 as a private motorsport club.
It has significant elevation change for a circuit of its length, with a blind crest on the back section.
The layout borrows corner shapes from several Formula One circuits, which is deliberate.
atlanta.overtaking: Into the hairpin, and into turn one.
sectors: the climb through the opening corners
the crest and the esses
the hairpin and the run to the line

nola.name: NOLA Motorsports Park
nola.character: A flat Louisiana circuit with a lot of corners and very little elevation — rhythm and patience rather than bravery.
facts: NOLA Motorsports Park sits just outside New Orleans and opened in 2011.
The circuit is almost completely flat, which is unusual and puts everything into the corner sequences.
It has hosted IndyCar, in a race remembered mostly for the weather.
nola.overtaking: Into turn one, and into the hairpin.
sectors: the opening corners
the flat infield section
the final complex onto the straight

palmbeach.name: Palm Beach
palmbeach.character: A flat, tight Florida club circuit — short lap, constant direction changes, and no room to relax.
facts: Palm Beach International Raceway has run in various forms since the 1960s and includes a drag strip alongside the road course.
The road course is flat and technical, with a short lap that puts cars into traffic quickly.
The road course shares the site with a drag strip, which is why the main straight is as wide and as flat as it is.
palmbeach.overtaking: Into the hairpin, and into turn one.
sectors: the first corners
the technical middle
the run to the line
